references.text: A curse on the one who leads a blind person astray, which directly relates to the prohibition against placing obstacles before the blind.
The same chapter contains the command to fear God, which also concludes verse 14.
Uses the same expression 'you shall fear your God' in connection with how one treats other people.
Repeats the phrase 'fear your God' in the context of fair treatment of others.
Again, the fear of God is linked to the ethical treatment of vulnerable people.
Prohibition against oppressing or exploiting vulnerable groups such as foreigners.
Describes the blind person groping in darkness, relevant for the protection of those with visual impairments.
A proverb about the one who stumbles over an obstacle, thematically linked to not placing stumbling blocks.
A prophetic call to remove obstacles from the people's path.
Warning against placing stumbling blocks before others; the same Hebrew word (מִכְשֹׁל) is used.
Paul urges not to place a stumbling block (πρόσκομμα) for a brother, reflecting the principle from Leviticus.
Continues the theme of not being the cause of others stumbling.
Warning that one's freedom becomes a stumbling block (πρόσκομμα) for the weak.
